paragraphs.heading: Power from the tide
paragraphs.text: Tidal power, also called tidal energy, means turning the energy of the tides into a useful form of power, which mostly means electricity. It is not yet widely used, but it has potential for generating electricity in the future. One advantage is predictability: the wind and the sun are harder to forecast than the tides.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy comes from
paragraphs.text: Tidal forces come from periodic variations in the gravitational pull of celestial bodies. These forces set the world’s oceans moving, and sea levels change periodically as the Earth rotates. The changes are highly regular and predictable, because the Earth’s spin and the Moon’s path around it follow a consistent pattern. No other technology draws on the energy held in the orbits of the Earth–Moon system and, to a smaller degree, the Earth–Sun system. Fossil fuel, wind, wave and solar energy, by contrast, originate directly or indirectly from the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: From tide mills to power stations
paragraphs.text: The idea is old. Tide mills were used in Europe and along North America’s Atlantic coast, and the earliest date from the Middle Ages or even Roman times. Incoming water was held in big storage ponds. When the tide went out, the water turned waterwheels that milled grain. The first large-scale tidal power plant in the world was the Rance Tidal Power Station in France, which became operational in 1966. It stayed the largest by output until August 2011, when South Korea opened the Sihwa Lake station, with 10 turbines generating 254 MW.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to catch a tide
paragraphs.text: Tidal stream generators power their turbines with the kinetic energy of moving water, much as wind turbines use the wind. Straits and inlets can create high water velocities at particular sites, and turbines can capture them. Tidal barrages instead use the potential energy in the height difference between high and low tide. A barrage is essentially a dam that spans the whole width of a tidal estuary. The incoming tide is led into a large basin behind the dam. As the tide recedes, the water is released through large turbines, and generators turn that motion into electrical power.

paragraphs.heading: Limits and promise
paragraphs.text: Among renewable sources, tidal energy has long been held back by relatively high cost and by a shortage of sites with high enough tidal ranges or flow velocities. Greater tidal variation and faster tidal currents can dramatically increase what a site can offer. Recent developments in design and in turbine technology indicate that far more tidal power may be available than was previously assumed, and that its costs, both economic and environmental, may fall to competitive levels. Tidal energy is also highly reliable and durable, with excellent energy density.

paragraphs.heading: Slowing the Earth
paragraphs.text: As the tides move, the Earth–Moon system loses mechanical energy. That loss has slowed the Earth’s rotation over the 4.5 billion years since the planet formed. During the last 620 million years the length of a day has grown from 21.9 hours to 24 hours. Tidal power will draw a little more energy out of the system. The effect is negligible, though, and nobody would notice it in the foreseeable future.
